etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle French germe, from Latin germen (“bud, seed, embryo”). Doublet of germen.

definitions.definition: The embryo of a seed, especially of a seed used as a cereal or grain. See Wikipedia article on cereal germ.
(biology) The small mass of cells from which a part of an organism develops, or a macroscopic but immature form of that part; a bud.
(biology) The small mass of cells from which a new organism develops; a seed, bud, spore, or zygote.
A pathogen: a pathogenic microorganism, such as a bacterium or virus.

quote.citation: 1895, H. G. Wells, The Stolen Bacillus:
quote.text: 'This again,' said the Bacteriologist, slipping a glass slide under the microscope, 'is a preparation of the celebrated Bacillus of cholera - the cholera germ.'

definitions.definition: (figurative) The origin or earliest version of an idea or project.

quote.citation: 1899 February, Joseph Conrad, “The Heart of Darkness”, in Blackwood’s Edinburgh Magazine, volume CLXV, number M, New York, N.Y.: The Leonard Scott Publishing Company, […], →OCLC, part I, page 194:
quote.text: What greatness had not floated on the ebb of that river into the mystery of an unknown earth? - the dreams of men, the seed of commonwealths, the germs of empires.

definitions.definition: (mathematics) An equivalence class that includes a specified function defined in an open neighborhood.

quote.text: Thus tempted, the lust to avenge me / Germed inly and grew.

quote.citation: 2011, Black Eyed Peas, Just Can't Get Enough:
quote.text: I’m addicted, want to germ inside your love
